title: She Says She's Fine

patient.name: Mdm Chia Bee Lian
patient.presenting_complaint: Here for a routine diabetic eye screening; appears well and walks in independently

history.hpc: Mdm Chia attends for routine diabetic eye screening. She looks well and walks in without aids. On routine fall-risk screening she initially brushes it off: 'Aiya I'm okay one lah.' On gentle questioning she admits: 'But last week I almost fall in the toilet, luckily I grab the rail. And I just started new sleeping pill, sometimes morning still groggy.' No injury occurred. She will be dilated today for the screening.
history.pmhx: Type 2 diabetes. Insomnia, recently started a sleeping tablet.
history.social_hx: Lives with husband. Works as a part-time cleaner. Came alone today.

examination_findings.fundus: For dilated diabetic screening by doctor/photography

investigations.fall_risk_assessment: Risk identified on screening despite a well appearance: a recent near-fall within the past week, a newly started sedative (zolpidem) with morning grogginess, and planned dilation today which will blur vision and increase photosensitivity.

diagnosis: A patient who looks low risk but is not — screening uncovered a recent near-fall and a new sedative, and planned dilation will add acute risk. This illustrates why ALL patients must be screened for fall risk at every visit, not only those who look frail.

immediate: Screen every patient for fall risk regardless of how well they appear, and ask specifically about recent falls/near-falls and new medications
Recognise the recent near-fall, new sedative, and planned dilation as genuine risk factors
Advise her that her vision will blur after dilation and to move carefully and ask for help while waiting
Seat her in a safe area and offer sunglasses/UV protectors after dilation
Flag to the nurse/doctor that she is now higher risk due to the near-fall and new sedative
Document the fall risk assessment, the factors uncovered, and the actions taken
follow_up: Doctor to proceed with the dilated diabetic screening
Advise her to mention the near-fall and the new sleeping tablet to her regular doctor
Arrange for her to be escorted out post-dilation and advise a companion for future dilated visits
patient_education: Explain kindly that even people who feel fine can be at risk, which is why we always ask
Advise her that the new sleeping pill can cause morning grogginess and to be careful, especially at night/in the toilet
Explain post-dilation blurring and photosensitivity (4-6 hours) and to avoid driving
Encourage simple home safety (grab bars, good lighting) and bringing a companion when dilated

key_points: Screens for fall risk despite the patient appearing well
Asks specifically about recent falls or near-falls
Identifies the newly started sedative and morning grogginess
Notes that dilation is planned today, adding acute risk
Performs and documents a fall risk assessment at this visit for ALL patients
Uncovers hidden risk factors through targeted questioning
Recognises the combination (near-fall, sedative, planned dilation) raises her risk
Understands that a well appearance does not exclude fall risk
Correctly identifies the patient as at-risk after screening
Recognises medication and dilation as modifiable/acute contributors
Applies the principle that all patients are screened every visit
Acts on the identified risk (safe seating, sunglasses, escort, staff alerted)
Educates the patient sensitively without dismissing her 'I'm fine' response
Documents the assessment and the factors uncovered
Advises follow-up with her regular doctor about the near-fall and new sedative
